sections.title: Taxonomy and general form
sections.text: Russula laricina Velen. is a brittlegill in the family Russulaceae (Basidiomycota). Its fruit body is small to medium-sized: the cap is often about 3–7 cm wide, convex at first, then expanded and usually depressed in the centre at maturity, sometimes with a low umbo. The cap cuticle is shiny and sticky in wet weather; its margin becomes distinctly grooved with age. Colour is highly variable: vinaceous red, purple, purplish brown, yellow ochre to ochre brown, sometimes with olive tones.

sections.title: Gills and stem
sections.text: The gills are rather spaced and fragile, often forked or joined by veins; they change from cream to yellow and sometimes pale orange. The fragile white stem is cylindrical to slightly club-shaped, approximately 3–7 × 1–1.5 cm; it may become spongy and then hollow, and turn grey with age or moisture. The white flesh is brittle and may also grey. The spore print is yellow.

sections.title: Ecology and identification
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal brittlegill is associated mainly with larches (Larix). A recent molecular study identified it among the frequent mycorrhizal partners of European larch (Larix decidua) in Alpine forests; mycological observations also report it, more rarely, under other conifers. Field descriptions place fruiting mainly from summer into autumn, varying by region. Cap colour alone cannot identify the species: R. laricina is variable and can be difficult to distinguish from R. nauseosa; microscopic examination and ecological context may be needed.

sections.title: Limits of this profile
sections.text: Taxonomic limits and reported characters vary among field guides and populations, especially for closely related species. This entry summarizes published characters and does not replace a full mycological identification. The consulted sources do not agree on culinary status, so edibility is not assessed here.

traits: Brittlegill in the family Russulaceae, with brittle flesh and no ring or volva
Cap usually 3–7 cm wide, convex then expanded and depressed in the centre; margin grooved with age
Highly variable colour, including copper-brown to ochre-brown forms as well as vinaceous red, purple or olive tones
Fragile, rather spaced gills, often forked or anastomosing, cream then yellow to pale ochre
Fragile white stem, sometimes becoming hollow and greying with age; yellow spore print
Ectomycorrhizal species mainly associated with larches (Larix); close species can be difficult to separate
safetyNote: Do not identify or eat a mushroom from this profile or a photograph. Sources disagree about the food use of Russula laricina; no edibility advice is given.
